etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English subordinat, from Medieval Latin subōrdinātus, past participle of subōrdināre, from sub- + ōrdināre (“to order”).

definitions.definition: Placed in a lower class, rank, or position.

quote.citation: 1695, John Woodward, “(please specify the page)”, in An Essay toward a Natural History of the Earth: And Terrestrial Bodies, Especially Minerals: […], London:  […]  Ric[hard] Wilkin […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The several kinds  […]  and subordinate species of each are easily known.

definitions.definition: Submissive or inferior to, or controlled by authority.

quote.citation: November 9, 1662, Robert South, Of the Creation of Man in the Image of God
quote.text: It was subordinate, not enslaved, to the understanding.

definitions.definition: (grammar, of a clause, not comparable) dependent on and either modifying or complementing the main clause
(transitive, grammar) To embed (a clause) into another clause that is the main one.
(transitive, finance) To make of lower priority in order of payment in bankruptcy.
(transitive) To treat (someone) as of less value or importance.
